investigations: the script asks for none
the opening words are put together from sentences of the script's read-aloud part, none changed

scenario.reasoning: A day and a half of sore throat, blocked and running nose, sneezing, dry cough and aching, with ill contacts and no feature of a chest infection: a common cold. The noise is the patient, who demands the strongest antibiotic before a flight and a meeting, and who has a penicillin allergy he will not mention. A learner is most likely to miss asking about allergies.

patient.name: Mr Julian Ashworth-Bell
patient.manner: Brisk and impatient, used to being deferred to, not abusive. He says so when he thinks a question is beside the point.

scenario.opening_words: Look, I've got about ten minutes, so let's be efficient. I've come down with something. So what I need is a course of antibiotics. The strong ones.

facts.fact: It started yesterday morning with a scratchy throat, and by last night I was blocked solid, sneezing, streaming, the whole business.
My head is pounding, I ache all over, and I feel absolutely wretched.
I am on a flight to New York tonight and I am in front of the board at nine tomorrow morning.
I had something in Dubai a few years ago, big white tablets, and it cleared up in two days.
I do not want to be told to rest and drink fluids. Resting is not on the table this week.
A dry, tickly cough started last night.
I feel hot and cold in turns, but I have not taken my temperature and I have had no shivering attacks.
I am not breathless, I have no chest pain, I am not coughing anything up and I have no wheeze.
I have no ear pain, no stiff neck and no rash.
My voice is a little hoarse. I am eating less but drinking normally.
Two colleagues and my fourteen-year-old daughter had the same thing last week.
My only ongoing condition is high blood pressure, diagnosed three years ago. I take lisinopril 10 mg once a day. I have no asthma or other chest disease.
I am recorded as allergic to penicillin. I was given it as a small child and came out in a rash. I was six, it was probably measles. Put me down as fine.
I took paracetamol and ibuprofen yesterday, which helped a little.
I stopped smoking twelve years ago, after about ten years of fifteen a day.
I drink two or three glasses of wine most evenings, and considerably more when I am entertaining clients.
I had a flu jab at the office in October. No recent Covid vaccination. No travel beyond the usual business trips.
My father had a heart attack at sixty-two. My mother is alive and well.
I am married with two children. I work seventy-hour weeks and sleep about five hours a night.

scenario.ideas: I believe this is a chest infection, and antibiotics are the obvious answer.
scenario.concerns: I cannot do this meeting sounding like this, and I do not have the luxury of waiting it out.
scenario.expectations: A course of antibiotics, the strong ones, today. Not a leaflet.
scenario.hidden_agenda: I was passed over for promotion last year. This meeting is the one that decides the next one. I am frightened of standing up tomorrow and being visibly diminished.

examination.finding: Slightly red. Normal tonsils, no exudate.

differential.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (the common cold)
Community-acquired pneumonia, considered and excluded on the history

plan.step: No antibiotic, with a plain explanation that antibiotics do not shorten a viral illness
Symptomatic treatment: regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, fluids, a decongestant, saline or steam for the nose
Advice for the flight: a decongestant before descent, and swallowing or the Valsalva manoeuvre
If a back-up or delayed prescription is agreed, it must not be a penicillin
Record the request for antibiotics, the decision not to prescribe and the reason given

scenario.safety_net: A high fever, breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood, symptoms that worsen after day five or have not settled by day ten: he should be seen, wherever he is.

data_gathering: Ask about breathlessness, chest pain and coughing anything up.
Ask about fever, and whether he has measured his temperature.
Ask about other illnesses and regular medicines.
Ask whether anyone around him has been ill.
Examine: temperature, pulse, breathing rate, oxygen level and the chest.
management: Do not prescribe an antibiotic on this history.
Explain that an antibiotic would not make him better by tomorrow.
Give advice on treating the symptoms, and for the flight.
If a back-up prescription is given, it is not a penicillin.
Tell him exactly what should make him seek help.
relating: Find the worry behind the demand.
Stay courteous under pressure and do not give way.
Say honestly how the illness will run.
